title: Advanced Linux Administration
subtitle: Jeopardy Review — Practice Set B

jeopardyFormatExample.clueText: This command streams the LAST 10 lines of a file and, with -f, follows a live log

categoryLegend: Files & Archives: tail, cp -a, rmdir, stat, gzip.  Permissions & ACLs: chmod, SUID, umask, setfacl -x, ls -l + (ACL flag).  Networking & DNS: ip addr, ping -c, A records, /etc/hosts, Ctrl-Z.  System & Shell: /etc/passwd, free, top, expr, shebang.  Boot, Services & Legacy: GRUB, chkconfig on, rcapache2 restart, iftop, scp.

clues.clue: This command streams the LAST 10 lines of a file by default and, with -f, follows a growing log live.
clues.explain: tail prints the last 10 lines by default (-n N for more); with -f it follows a file live -- the standard way to watch a growing log.

clues.clue: This cp flag performs an archive copy: recursive, and preserving timestamps, ownership, symlinks, and permissions.
clues.explain: cp -a copies a directory tree recursively while preserving timestamps, ownership, symlinks, and permissions -- ideal for a faithful backup.

clues.clue: This command removes an EMPTY directory and fails if the directory still contains any files.
clues.explain: rmdir removes only an empty directory and errors otherwise; use rm -r to delete a directory together with its contents.

clues.clue: This command displays a file's full metadata -- size, inode, permissions, and its access, modify, and change timestamps.
clues.explain: stat shows a file's complete metadata, including the three timestamps (atime/mtime/ctime) -- far more detail than ls -l.

clues.clue: This compression tool shrinks a single file in place, appending .gz; combined with tar it yields a .tar.gz tarball.
clues.explain: gzip compresses one file to .gz; pair it with tar (tar -czf) to produce a compressed .tar.gz archive of many files at once.

clues.clue: This command sets a file's read/write/execute permission bits using symbolic (u+x) or octal (755) notation.
clues.explain: chmod sets the permission bits via symbolic (u+x, go-w) or octal (755, 644) notation; it changes the mode, not ownership.

clues.clue: Set on an executable, this special permission bit makes the program run with the privileges of its owner -- e.g. passwd runs as root.
clues.explain: The SUID bit makes an executable run as its owner rather than the caller; /usr/bin/passwd uses it so users can update root-owned /etc/shadow.

clues.clue: This shell setting defines which permission bits are stripped from newly created files and directories by default.
clues.explain: umask removes bits from the default mode of new files/dirs; a umask of 022 yields 644 files and 755 directories.

clues.clue: This setfacl option REMOVES a specific named-user or named-group entry from a file's access control list.
clues.explain: setfacl -x removes one named ACL entry; setfacl -b strips ALL extended ACL entries at once, leaving the base owner/group/other.

clues.clue: In ls -l output, this single character appended right after the rwx permission string reveals that a file carries an extended ACL -- run getfacl to read it.
clues.explain: A trailing + on the ls -l mode (e.g. -rw-rw-r--+) flags an extended ACL; getfacl then reads the full named-user/group entries behind it.

clues.clue: This ip subcommand lists every interface with its assigned IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, replacing ifconfig run with no arguments.
clues.explain: ip addr (show) lists interfaces and their addresses; it is the modern replacement for the deprecated ifconfig with no arguments.

clues.clue: This ping flag sends a fixed COUNT of echo requests and then stops automatically with a summary.
clues.explain: ping -c N sends exactly N packets then exits with a summary -- unlike -w, which stops after a time deadline regardless of count.

clues.clue: This DNS record type maps a fully qualified hostname directly to an IPv4 address.
clues.explain: An A record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address (AAAA does the same for IPv6); it is the fundamental forward-lookup record.

clues.clue: Before querying DNS, the resolver checks this local file of static hostname-to-IP mappings.
clues.explain: /etc/hosts holds static hostname-to-IP mappings the resolver checks before DNS; lookup order is set by /etc/nsswitch.conf.

clues.clue: Pressing this key combination suspends the foreground process and returns you to the shell, leaving the job stopped.
clues.explain: Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP, suspending the foreground job and returning the shell; resume it with fg (foreground) or bg (background).

clues.clue: This system file lists every user account, one per line, with username, UID, GID, home directory, and login shell.
clues.explain: /etc/passwd lists every account (username, UID, GID, GECOS, home, shell); password hashes live separately in /etc/shadow.

clues.clue: This command reports total, used, and available physical RAM and swap in a quick one-shot table.
clues.explain: free reports total/used/free RAM and swap (add -h for human units) -- the quick memory snapshot, versus top's continuous live view.

clues.clue: This interactive command shows a live, continuously updating view of processes ranked by CPU or memory use.
clues.explain: top is the interactive live process monitor, sortable by CPU or memory; htop is a friendlier color variant of the same idea.

clues.clue: This command evaluates a simple arithmetic or string expression and prints the result, e.g. expr 3 + 4.
clues.explain: expr evaluates an arithmetic or string expression and prints the result; modern scripts more often use $(( )) or the let builtin.

clues.clue: This two-character sequence at the very top of a script, followed by an interpreter path, tells the kernel which program runs the file.
clues.explain: The shebang (#!) on line 1, followed by an interpreter path like /bin/bash, tells the kernel which program should execute the script.

clues.clue: This is the standard Linux boot loader that presents the kernel-selection menu and loads the kernel at startup.
clues.explain: GRUB is the standard Linux boot loader: it shows the kernel menu, loads the chosen kernel and initramfs, then hands off to init/systemd.

clues.clue: This legacy SysV command ADDS the apache2 service to the init runlevels so it starts at boot. (Modern: systemctl enable apache2)
clues.response: What is chkconfig apache2 on? (modern: systemctl enable apache2)
clues.explain: chkconfig <svc> on adds a service to the SysV runlevels so it auto-starts at boot; the systemd equivalent is systemctl enable.

clues.clue: On SUSE SysV systems, this rc-style wrapper stops and then starts the apache2 service in one step. (Modern: systemctl restart apache2)
clues.response: What is rcapache2 restart? (modern: systemctl restart apache2)
clues.explain: SUSE's rc<service> scripts wrap the SysV init script; 'restart' stops then starts the daemon. systemd uses systemctl restart.

clues.clue: This modern terminal tool shows live per-connection bandwidth usage, sorted by throughput -- a successor to older traffic visualizers.
clues.explain: iftop shows live per-connection bandwidth in the terminal, sorted by throughput -- a modern replacement for older traffic-visualizer tools.

clues.clue: This OpenSSH utility copies individual files between hosts over an encrypted SSH connection.
clues.explain: scp copies files between hosts over SSH (encrypted); for large trees or repeated syncs, rsync is more efficient via delta transfer.
